purpose: One combined source-first inventory covering the 66 Area-2 decision paths that B3-C and B3-D together require, so B3-C does not finish only for B3-D to discover no remaining capacity.

method.granularity: CMR paragraph / statutory subsection, not regulation number
method.area_assignment_rule: Classify from the actual tested competency and existing bank precedent, never from the regulation number. A source is not usable merely because it is unused.
method.verbatim_rule: The controlling proposition must be verbatim-verifiable from an official primary or official government source before authoring. Section headings, corrupted partial text, secondary republication alone and search snippets alone are all rejected.

source_viability.publisher: Commonwealth of Massachusetts, official publisher of the General Laws
source_viability.retrieval: Browser, same-origin fetch, section text under the main paragraph nodes
source_viability.evidence: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19 retrieved in full and verbatim, including subsections (a) through (d). Subsection (a) states that a prescription for a controlled substance to be valid shall be issued for a legitimate medical purpose by a practitioner acting in the usual course of his professional practice, and that a corresponding responsibility shall rest with the pharmacist who fills the prescription.
source_viability.significance: This is the principal remaining Area-2 source. M.G.L. c. 94C and c. 112 pharmacist-practice provisions are fully available at paragraph granularity.
source_viability.note_on_urls: Section URLs that carry a fraction in the section number, for example c. 112 s. 24B one-half, do not resolve under the naive tilde-two encoding and must be located from the chapter index.

source_viability.correction_note: Provenance cleanup only, made after the CLAUDE-FRESH-B3A-R1 official-source cure. No question, hash, rule or legal conclusion was mutated because of this wording change. No claim is made about which extraction implementation is superior.

source_viability.evidence: Section 9.15(1) and (2) retrieved verbatim and used to repair MA-Q-0288.
source_viability.area_capacity_finding: Largely exhausted as an Area-2 source. Bank precedent puts 9.02 and 9.04 in Area 4, 9.14 and 9.17 in Area 3, 9.19 and 9.24 in Area 4, and 9.21 and 9.23 in Area 1. Of the sections with no question at all, compliance packaging, emergency kits, automated systems, records, non-resident pharmacies, storage, plans of correction and generic interchange all sit in Area 4 by precedent. Clearly Area-2 headroom is limited to 9.03 Advertising plus unkeyed paragraphs of 9.01, 9.13 and 9.15.

Probes for the termination terms and for the agreement filed in the primary practice setting return nothing, so parts of 16.04 are absent from the extraction.
source_viability.controller_decision: Do NOT author 16.03 or 16.04 propositions from this extraction. De-kerned text is reconstruction, not verbatim verification, and the governing instruction forbids authoring from corrupted partial text. An alternative official rendering must be found before 16.03 and 16.04 can be counted toward Area-2 capacity.
source_viability.impact: 247 CMR 16.04 is the single richest untapped CDTM source, covering required agreement terms, duties, biennial renewal, termination, filing in the primary practice setting and employment relationships. Losing it materially reduces the Area-2 candidate pool, so its recovery is a priority for the remainder of the census.

source_classification_surveys.finding: Most of c. 94C's pharmacist-facing content classifies to Area 3 Dispensing Requirements by this bank's precedent, not to Area 2 Pharmacist Practice. Area 2 in this bank means the pharmacist's own professional practice: counselling, administration, pharmacist prescribing, validity determinations as professional judgment, professional conduct and public-health roles. It does not mean dispensing mechanics.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2 (Pharmacist collaborative practice agreements; collaborative drug therapy management)
families.exact_section: 24B1/2(a), definition of collaborative drug therapy management
families.operative_proposition: CDTM is the initiating, monitoring, modifying and discontinuing of a patient's drug therapy by a pharmacist in accordance with a collaborative practice agreement; it may include collecting and reviewing patient histories, obtaining and checking vital signs, and, under the supervision of or in direct consultation with a physician, ordering and evaluating the results of laboratory tests directly related to drug therapy when performed in accordance with approved protocols applicable to the practice setting and when the evaluation shall not include a diagnostic component.
families.trigger: pharmacist proposes to order or interpret a laboratory test while co-managing therapy
families.professional_decision: decide whether the proposed act falls inside CDTM or crosses into diagnosis
conditions: under physician supervision or in direct consultation
test directly related to drug therapy
performed under approved protocols applicable to the practice setting
exceptions: the evaluation shall not include a diagnostic component
families.why_area_2: Tests the outer boundary of the pharmacist's own professional practice, which is Area 2 competency, not facility operations or a dispensing mechanic.
families.family_novelty: MA-Q-0081 keys the s. 24B1/2(b) qualification list and MA-Q-0082 keys the retail disease-scope limit. Neither touches the outer boundary of the CDTM definition itself, where the pharmacist may order and evaluate laboratory results but the evaluation may not include a diagnostic component.
families.scenario_sketch: A collaborating pharmacist reviewing a co-managed patient's laboratory results is asked to say what the abnormal result means for an undiagnosed symptom. The candidate must separate the permitted evaluation of a test directly related to drug therapy from the prohibited diagnostic component.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2 (Pharmacist collaborative practice agreements; collaborative drug therapy management)
families.operative_proposition: A collaborative practice agreement is a written and signed agreement between a pharmacist with training and experience relevant to the scope of the collaborative practice and a supervising physician that defines the collaborative practice. The collaborative practice shall be within the scope of the supervising physician's practice. Each collaborative practice agreement shall be subject to review and renewal on a biennial basis. A collaborative practice agreement shall include individually developed guidelines for any prescriptive practice of the pharmacist.
families.trigger: an agreement is drafted, or is reaching its second anniversary
families.professional_decision: decide whether the agreement is validly constituted and still current
conditions: written and signed
within the supervising physician's own scope of practice
biennial review and renewal
individually developed guidelines for any prescriptive practice
families.why_area_2: Turns on the pharmacist's authority to act at all, which is a practice-competency question.
families.family_novelty: MA-Q-0081 keys the pharmacist's personal qualifications. This keys the agreement's own constitution instead: written and signed, within the supervising physician's scope, biennially reviewed and renewed, and carrying individually developed guidelines for prescriptive practice.
families.scenario_sketch: An agreement signed 26 months ago has never been reviewed and covers a therapy area outside the supervising physician's own practice. The pharmacist must decide whether they may still act under it.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2 (Pharmacist collaborative practice agreements; collaborative drug therapy management)
families.operative_proposition: A patient is a person referred to a pharmacist by his supervising physician for the purpose of receiving CDTM services. The supervising physician shall assess the patient and include a diagnosis when referring the patient to the collaborating pharmacist. The patient shall be notified of, and shall consent to, the CDTM services in the retail drug business setting. Individual referral and consent shall be recorded by the pharmacist and the supervising physician in the patient's record.
families.trigger: a person presents for CDTM services without a completed referral or recorded consent
families.professional_decision: decide whether this person is a CDTM patient the pharmacist may co-manage
conditions: physician assessment and diagnosis in the referral
notice and consent in the retail drug business setting
referral and consent recorded by BOTH pharmacist and physician in the patient record
exceptions: the express notice-and-consent limb is written for the retail drug business setting
families.why_area_2: The pharmacist must decide whether a patient in front of them is eligible for their own service.
families.family_novelty: MA-Q-0082 assumes a completed referral and consent and then keys the disease-scope decision. This keys the constitution of the referral itself: the physician must assess and include a diagnosis, and the referral and consent must be recorded by BOTH the pharmacist and the physician in the patient record.
families.scenario_sketch: A referral arrives naming the therapy area but carrying no diagnosis, and the consent is noted only in the pharmacy's own file. The pharmacist must decide whether this person is yet a CDTM patient they may co-manage.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2 (Pharmacist collaborative practice agreements; collaborative drug therapy management)
families.exact_section: 24B1/2(c)(1) through (4), non-retail settings and their approval authorities
families.operative_proposition: CDTM shall only be allowed in the following settings: hospitals licensed under c. 111 s. 51, subject to approval by the medical staff executive committee or designee; long-term care facilities licensed under c. 111 s. 71, subject to approval by the medical director or designee; inpatient or outpatient hospice settings licensed under c. 111 s. 57D, subject to approval by the hospice's medical director or designee; ambulatory care clinics licensed under c. 111 s. 51, with on-site supervision by the attending physician and a collaborating pharmacist, subject to approval by the medical staff executive committee or designee, or medical director or designee.
families.trigger: a CDTM arrangement is proposed in a particular care setting
families.professional_decision: identify whose approval the setting requires and whether on-site supervision applies
conditions: setting must be one of the enumerated licensed settings
the approving body differs by setting
ambulatory care clinics additionally require on-site supervision by the attending physician and a collaborating pharmacist
families.why_area_2: The pharmacist decides whether they may practise CDTM here and on whose authority; this is scope of the pharmacist's own practice rather than facility licensure.
families.family_novelty: The existing CDTM questions are all retail-setting. This keys the four non-retail settings and the fact that the approving body differs by setting, with ambulatory care clinics additionally requiring on-site supervision.
families.scenario_sketch: A pharmacist is asked to start CDTM in an ambulatory care clinic on the strength of the hospital medical staff executive committee's earlier approval. The candidate must identify whose approval this setting needs and that on-site supervision applies.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2 (Pharmacist collaborative practice agreements; collaborative drug therapy management)
families.operative_proposition: A collaborating pharmacist in a retail drug business, with supervision by a physician according to the terms of the collaborative practice agreement, is limited to patients 18 years of age or older and to an extension by 30 days of current drug therapy prescribed by the supervising physician.
families.actor: collaborating pharmacist in a retail drug business
families.trigger: a referred retail patient needs continued therapy or is under 18
families.professional_decision: decide whether the patient and the proposed extension are inside the retail limits
conditions: patients 18 years of age or older
extension limited to 30 days
the therapy extended must be current therapy prescribed by the supervising physician
families.why_area_2: A pharmacist-side authority limit exercised at the point of care.
families.family_novelty: The retail paragraph is shared with MA-Q-0082, but the keyed discrimination is different. MA-Q-0082 keys disease scope. This keys the patient-age floor and the fact that the retail power is an extension of existing physician-prescribed therapy limited to 30 days. The 30-day figure appears in MA-Q-0083 only as an unkeyed distractor.
families.scenario_sketch: A 16-year-old referred patient needs their current therapy continued for 60 days while the physician is away. The candidate must apply both the age floor and the 30-day extension limit.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2 (Pharmacist collaborative practice agreements; collaborative drug therapy management)
families.exact_section: 24B1/2(c)(5), retail disease-state list and specific reference requirement
families.operative_proposition: In the retail setting the collaborating pharmacist is limited to administration of vaccines or the modification of dosages of medications prescribed by the supervising physician for asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, congestive heart failure, HIV or AIDS, osteoporosis and co-morbidities identified by the supervising physician for the individual patient along with the primary diagnosis. The collaborative practice agreement shall specifically reference each disease state being co-managed.
families.actor: collaborating pharmacist in a retail drug business
families.trigger: a dosage modification is proposed for a condition
families.professional_decision: decide whether the condition is inside the retail list and specifically referenced in the agreement
conditions: condition on the enumerated list, or a co-morbidity identified by the physician for that patient
the agreement must specifically reference each disease state co-managed
families.why_area_2: A clinical-authority boundary the pharmacist applies personally.
families.rejection_reason: MA-Q-0082 already keys exactly this discrimination. Its key is to continue the referred hypertension management and return new wheezing to the physician rather than treat it as an eligible retail disease state, which is the disease-state-list and specific-reference test. Counting it again would be a paraphrase of a released question.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2 (Pharmacist collaborative practice agreements; collaborative drug therapy management)
families.operative_proposition: A retail drug business practicing in collaborative drug therapy management under this section shall not be required to register as a Health Facility under 105 CMR 700.004(A)(2)(d).
families.actor: retail drug business engaging in CDTM
families.trigger: a pharmacy is advised it must add a Health Facility registration before starting CDTM
families.professional_decision: decide whether the additional registration is in fact required
exceptions: the carve-out applies to a retail drug business practising CDTM under this section
families.why_area_2: Borderline. The proposition is about a registration obligation rather than a pharmacist practice decision, which points at Area 4 by bank precedent for facility registration items.
families.rejection_reason: A facility registration obligation. This bank places facility registration in Area 4, and a source shortage must not be solved by relabelling Area-4 content as Area 2.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2 (Pharmacist collaborative practice agreements; collaborative drug therapy management)
families.operative_proposition: A physician or a physician group may hire pharmacists for the purpose of practicing collaborative drug therapy management under a collaborative practice agreement for the benefit of a patient of that physician or physician group. No retail pharmacy may employ a physician for the purpose of maintaining, establishing or entering into a collaborative practice agreement with a patient. Nothing shall prohibit a retail pharmacy from hiring a physician or licensed medical practitioner for the purpose of conducting quality assurance reviews of its pharmacists that are engaged in the practice of collaborative drug therapy.
families.actor: collaborating pharmacist and the employing entity
families.trigger: a retail pharmacy proposes to employ a physician in connection with CDTM
families.professional_decision: decide which direction of employment the statute permits and for what purpose
conditions: physician or physician group may hire pharmacists for CDTM
exceptions: a retail pharmacy may hire a physician for quality assurance review of its CDTM pharmacists, but not for maintaining, establishing or entering into a collaborative practice agreement
families.why_area_2: The prohibition governs the integrity of the pharmacist's collaborative practice, which the pharmacist must be able to apply; the bank places professional-conduct limits in Area 2.
families.family_novelty: The bank's professional-conduct items concern remuneration for referrals and institutional dispensing limits. This keys the direction and purpose of employment in collaborative practice: a physician may hire pharmacists, a retail pharmacy may not employ a physician to establish an agreement, but may hire one for quality assurance review.
families.scenario_sketch: A retail chain proposes to put a physician on staff so that its pharmacists can enter collaborative agreements in-house, and separately to have that physician review their CDTM casework. The candidate must separate the prohibited purpose from the permitted one.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, ss. 19A, 19B and 19E (statewide standing-order regimes)
families.operative_proposition: Before dispensing emergency contraception under s. 19A a pharmacist MAY complete a commissioner-approved training program. Before dispensing a COVID-19 drug under s. 19E a pharmacist SHALL complete a commissioner-approved training program that includes evaluation of the patient's medical history and relevant records including recent laboratory blood work for kidney or liver problems, clinical considerations relative to contraindications with commonly prescribed medications, recommendations for clinical monitoring for side effects and appropriate recommendation that the patient follow up with a medical practitioner.
families.actor: licensed pharmacist dispensing under a statewide standing order
families.trigger: pharmacist proposes to dispense under one of the standing-order regimes without having completed the relevant training
families.professional_decision: decide whether training is a precondition for this particular regime or merely available
conditions: the regime determines whether training is permissive or mandatory
the s. 19E training has prescribed content
families.why_area_2: A precondition on the pharmacist's own authority to act, exercised before any dispensing decision. The bank places naloxone and contraception pharmacist authority in Area 2.
families.family_novelty: The bank's naloxone and contraception questions key product status, third-party dispensing and protocol screening. None keys the training precondition, and none contrasts a permissive training regime with a mandatory one carrying prescribed content.
families.scenario_sketch: A pharmacist who has completed no commissioner-approved training is asked to dispense emergency contraception in the morning and Paxlovid in the afternoon, both under statewide standing orders. The candidate must see that only one of the two is blocked.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, ss. 19A(e), 19B(d) and 19E(d) (standing-order reporting and confidentiality)
families.exact_section: c. 94C s. 19B(d), compared with s. 19A(e) and s. 19E(d)
families.operative_proposition: A pharmacist who dispenses an opioid antagonist shall ANNUALLY report to the department the number of doses dispensed; reports shall not identify an individual patient, shall be confidential and shall not constitute a public record. Emergency contraception reporting under s. 19A(e) is likewise annual and confidential. COVID-19 control measure reporting under s. 19E(d) is instead made UPON REQUEST of the department.
families.actor: pharmacist who has dispensed under a statewide standing order
families.trigger: the department seeks dispensing data, or the reporting period closes
families.professional_decision: decide when the report is owed and what may be included or withheld
conditions: annual for opioid antagonists and emergency contraception
on request for COVID-19 control measures
no individual patient identification
exceptions: the reports are confidential and are not public records
families.why_area_2: A disclosure obligation owed personally by the dispensing pharmacist, and a confidentiality limit on what that disclosure may contain. Confidentiality and disclosure are named Area-2 themes and no question currently keys either.
families.family_novelty: No question in the bank keys a confidentiality or disclosure discrimination. The keyed axis here is the reporting cadence difference across the three regimes plus the bar on identifying an individual patient and the non-public-record status.
families.scenario_sketch: A pharmacy receives a public records request for its naloxone dispensing data alongside a departmental request for COVID-19 dispensing figures. The pharmacist must decide what is owed, to whom, and what may not be identified.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, ss. 19B(e) and 19E(e) (insurance handling before dispensing)
families.operative_proposition: A pharmacist or designee who dispenses an opioid antagonist shall, for health insurance billing and cost-sharing, treat the transaction as the dispensing of a prescription to the person purchasing it regardless of the ultimate user. Unless the purchaser requests to pay out-of-pocket, the pharmacist or designee shall make a reasonable effort to identify the purchaser's insurance coverage and to submit a claim to the carrier PRIOR TO dispensing.
families.actor: pharmacist or designee dispensing under the standing order
families.trigger: a third party presents to obtain naloxone for someone else
families.professional_decision: decide whose transaction this is for billing, and what must be attempted before the product is handed over
conditions: treated as a prescription to the purchaser regardless of ultimate user
reasonable effort to identify coverage and submit a claim before dispensing
exceptions: the purchaser requests to pay out-of-pocket
families.why_area_2: A pharmacist action required before dispensing, framed around the purchaser rather than the ultimate user, and turning on a patient election. It is a practice duty rather than a dispensing mechanic.
families.family_novelty: MA-Q-0097 keys third-party dispensing eligibility and MA-Q-0098 keys OTC versus prescription product status. Neither touches the billing-identity rule or the pre-dispensing claim attempt.
families.scenario_sketch: A parent asks for naloxone for an adult child and says nothing about payment. The pharmacist must decide whose insurance is relevant and what must happen before the product leaves the counter.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21A (prospective drug review and counselling)
families.operative_proposition: A pharmacist SHALL conduct a prospective drug review before each new prescription is dispensed or delivered to a patient or a person acting on behalf of such patient. Such review MAY include, but is not limited to, screening for therapeutic duplication, drug disease contraindication, drug interactions including serious interactions with nonprescription or over-the-counter drugs, incorrect drug dosage, duration of drug treatment, drug allergy interactions and clinical abuse or misuse.
families.trigger: a new prescription is about to be dispensed or delivered, including to an agent of the patient
families.professional_decision: decide that the review is mandatory while its listed content is a professional-judgment menu, and that delivery to an agent does not remove the duty
conditions: before each new prescription
applies to delivery to a person acting on behalf of the patient
exceptions: the section does not apply to a drug dispensed to an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home except as required by federal regulation
families.why_area_2: The pharmacist's own mandatory clinical review, distinct from dispensing mechanics. The bank already places counselling and professional judgment in Area 2.
families.family_novelty: The bank's Area-2 counselling questions key the offer, the trigger, the content menu and the consultation area. None keys the separate statutory prospective drug review, its mandatory character, or its application when an agent collects the prescription.
families.scenario_sketch: A neighbour collects a patient's first prescription for a new drug and declines counselling on the patient's behalf. The pharmacist must separate the review that is owed regardless from the counselling that was declined.

families.exact_section: c. 94C s. 21A, second and third paragraphs
families.operative_proposition: A pharmacist shall offer to counsel any person who presents a new prescription for filling. Such offer shall be made either by face to face communication between the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee and the patient, or by telephone, except when the patient's needs or availability require an alternative method of counselling. If a person elects delivery at a location other than a pharmacy, the requirements may be satisfied by providing access to a toll-free telephone service, and the number of that toll-free service shall be PRINTED ON A LABEL AFFIXED TO EACH CONTAINER of a prescription drug dispensed by a pharmacy to a patient.
families.trigger: a patient elects delivery away from the pharmacy, or the patient's needs make the ordinary methods unsuitable
families.professional_decision: decide which offer method the statute permits here, and what must appear on the container
conditions: face to face or telephone as the default methods
toll-free access for off-premises delivery
the toll-free number printed on a label affixed to each container
exceptions: an alternative method where the patient's needs or availability require it
families.why_area_2: The manner in which the pharmacist discharges a personal counselling duty, which the bank places in Area 2.
families.family_novelty: MA-Q-0213 keys that a remote-delivery offer is still required. This keys the permitted methods themselves, the needs-or-availability exception, and the separate container-labelling requirement for the toll-free number, none of which is keyed anywhere.
families.scenario_sketch: A pharmacy ships to a patient who is deaf and cannot use a telephone, and prints the toll-free number only on the bag insert. The candidate must resolve both the method question and the labelling defect.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21A (evidentiary presumption from the record)
families.operative_proposition: The pharmacist or designee shall make reasonable efforts to obtain, record and maintain the listed patient information, which may be recorded in the patient's manual or electronic profile, in the prescription signature log or in any other system of records. THE ABSENCE OF ANY RECORD OF A FAILURE TO ACCEPT THE PHARMACIST'S OFFER TO COUNSEL SHALL CREATE A PRESUMPTION THAT SUCH COUNSELLING WAS PROVIDED.
families.trigger: a later inquiry asks whether counselling was in fact provided on a past fill
families.professional_decision: understand which way the statutory presumption runs and what recording choice controls it
conditions: reasonable efforts to obtain, record and maintain
recording location is flexible
families.why_area_2: It governs the evidential consequence of the pharmacist's own counselling practice and record-keeping choices.
families.family_novelty: MA-Q-0086 keys documenting a declined offer. This keys the opposite direction: the statutory presumption that arises from the ABSENCE of a refusal record, which no question tests.
families.scenario_sketch: A complaint alleges a patient was never counselled on a fill from two years ago. The profile carries no refusal note. The pharmacist must say what the record's silence establishes.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19C (continuous supply of opioid antagonists)
families.operative_proposition: The board shall promulgate regulations requiring pharmacies located in areas with high incidence of opiate overdose to maintain a continuous supply of opioid antagonists including over-the-counter products, and such pharmacies shall notify the department if the supply or stock is insufficient to enable compliance.
families.trigger: stock of opioid antagonists runs short in a designated high-incidence area
families.professional_decision: n/a - the duty runs to the pharmacy as a facility
conditions: pharmacy located in a board-designated high-incidence area
families.why_area_2: It is not Area 2. The actor is the pharmacy and the duty is stocking and notification.
families.rejection_reason: A pharmacy stocking and notification obligation. This bank places inventory and facility duties in Area 4, and a capacity shortage must not be solved by relabelling Area-4 content as Area 2.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, ss. 19A(c), 19B(c) and 19E(c) (standing-order dispensing authority and immunity)
families.operative_proposition: A licensed pharmacist may dispense the relevant product in accordance with the statewide standing order, and except for gross negligence or wilful misconduct a pharmacist acting in good faith is not subject to criminal or civil liability or professional disciplinary action.
families.trigger: dispensing under a statewide standing order
families.professional_decision: identify the authority to dispense without an individual prescription and the limits of the liability shield
conditions: dispensing in accordance with the statewide standing order
acting in good faith
families.why_area_2: Pharmacist authority to act without an individual prescription.
families.rejection_category: overconcentration - structurally identical across three sections
families.rejection_reason: Sections 19A(c), 19B(c) and 19E(c) state the same authority-plus-immunity structure for three different products. Counting this as a family on top of the training, reporting and billing families drawn from the same cluster would test the same discrimination again with only the drug name changed. Recorded and rejected rather than counted.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19F (pharmacist prescribing of hormonal contraception)
families.operative_proposition: The rules shall require a pharmacist to refer the patient to the patient's primary care practitioner or reproductive health care practitioner, if applicable, upon prescribing and dispensing, or advise the patient to consult with such a practitioner; to provide the patient with a written record of the product prescribed and dispensed; and to dispense the product to the patient as soon as practicable after the pharmacist issues the prescription.
families.actor: pharmacist prescribing under the contraception pathway
families.trigger: the pharmacist has just issued a contraceptive prescription under the pathway
families.professional_decision: identify what the pharmacist still owes the patient after issuing, and how quickly the product must follow
conditions: referral or advice to consult
a written record of what was prescribed and dispensed
dispensing as soon as practicable after issuing
exceptions: the referral limb applies if the patient has such a practitioner
families.why_area_2: Duties attaching personally to the pharmacist's own prescribing act. The bank already places pharmacist contraceptive prescribing in Area 2.
families.family_novelty: MA-Q-0095 keys that a prior prescription is not required but screening still is. MA-Q-0096 keys the repeat clinical-visit bar. Neither touches the referral, written-record and prompt-dispensing duties that follow the prescribing act.
families.scenario_sketch: A pharmacist screens and prescribes, then tells the patient to collect the product next week and to raise it at her next physician visit whenever that happens. The candidate must identify which of the post-prescribing duties that fails.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19F (prohibitions on the prescribing pharmacist)
families.operative_proposition: The rules shall prohibit a pharmacist from requiring a patient to schedule an appointment with the pharmacist for the prescribing or dispensing of a hormonal contraceptive patch or self-administered oral hormonal contraceptive.
families.trigger: a pharmacy proposes to run the pathway by appointment only
families.professional_decision: recognise that access to the pathway may not be conditioned on an appointment
families.why_area_2: A prohibition on how the pharmacist may condition their own prescribing service.
families.family_novelty: Neither existing question touches the appointment prohibition. The keyed axis is a prohibition on the pharmacist rather than an eligibility condition on the patient.
families.scenario_sketch: A pharmacy posts that contraceptive consultations are by booked appointment only and turns away a walk-in. The candidate must identify the prohibition that defeats the policy.

families.source: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19F(c)(i)(A) and (B) (training and self-screening)
families.operative_proposition: The rules shall require a pharmacist to complete a board-approved training program related to prescribing these products, and to provide a self-screening risk assessment tool that the patient shall use prior to the pharmacist prescribing.
families.professional_decision: confirm the training precondition and the pre-prescribing screening step
conditions: board-approved training
patient completes the self-screening tool before prescribing
families.why_area_2: Preconditions on the pharmacist's own prescribing authority.
families.rejection_reason: MA-Q-0095 already keys that the screening and protocol process still applies even without a prior prescription, and its distractor E is the skip-the-self-screening error. Counting this would paraphrase a released question.
